chapters.title: The Defense
paragraphs: I don't know what impression my accusers have made on you, Athenians, but they almost made me forget who I was, they spoke so persuasively. Yet they have hardly said a word of truth. Of all their lies, one particularly astonished me: they warned you to be on your guard against being deceived by my eloquence. That seemed utterly shameless, since they knew they would be exposed as soon as I opened my mouth and showed that I was anything but a great speaker. Unless by eloquence they mean the power of truth. If that is what they mean, I admit I am eloquent, but in a very different way from them! As I said, they have scarcely spoken the truth at all, but from me you will hear the whole truth. It won't be delivered in their style, as a prepared speech decorated with fine words and phrases. No, by heaven! I will use whatever words and arguments come to me, because I am confident that my cause is just. (Another possible reading is: I am certain that this is the right approach.) At my age, Athenians, I should not stand before you like a young man showing off his oratory. Let no one expect that of me.

I must also ask you a favor. If I defend myself in my usual way, using the words you have heard me use in the marketplace, at the money-changers' tables, or anywhere else, please don't be surprised or interrupt me on that account. I am over seventy and appearing before a court for the first time, so its language is completely foreign to me. Treat me as you would a foreigner whom you would excuse for speaking his native language in the manner of his own country. Is that an unfair request? Disregard my manner of speaking, whether good or bad, and attend only to whether my words are true. Let the speaker speak truthfully and the judge decide justly.

First I must answer the old charges and my first accusers; then I will turn to the more recent ones. For many years, many people have been making false accusations against me to you. I fear them more than Anytus and his associates, though they too are dangerous in their own way. The others are much more dangerous. They began when you were children and took hold of your minds with their lies. They spoke of a certain Socrates, a wise man who speculated about the heavens, investigated what lay beneath the earth, and made the worse case appear the better one. It is the people who spread that story whom I fear, because their listeners tend to assume that anyone who investigates such things does not believe the gods exist. There are many of them, and their charges are old. They made them when you were more impressionable than now, in childhood or youth, and their case went unchallenged because no one answered it. Hardest of all, I do not know their names and cannot tell you who they are, except perhaps for a comic poet. All those who persuaded you out of envy and malice, some after first persuading themselves, are particularly difficult to deal with. I cannot bring them here and question them. I must defend myself against shadows, making my case when no one answers.

So please agree with me, as I said, that my opponents fall into two groups: the recent ones and the old ones. I hope you see why I should answer the older accusers first, since you heard their accusations long before the others and much more often.

Well then, I must defend myself and try, in a short time, to clear away a slander that has lasted a long time. May I succeed, if success would benefit you and me and help my case! The task is not easy; I understand that perfectly well. Leaving the outcome to God, I will now make my defense as the law requires.

Let me start at the beginning. What accusation gave rise to the slander against me and, in fact, encouraged Meletus to bring this charge? What do the slanderers say? Let them be my prosecutors, and let me sum up their words in a formal statement: 'Socrates does wrong and meddles in things beneath the earth and in the heavens; he makes the worse case appear the better one and teaches others these things.' That is the accusation. It is just what you have seen in Aristophanes' comedy _The Clouds_, where a man he calls Socrates claims to walk on air and talks nonsense about matters of which I claim to know neither much nor little. I do not mean to speak disparagingly of anyone who studies natural philosophy. I would be very sorry if Meletus could bring so serious a charge against me. But the plain truth, Athenians, is that I have nothing to do with speculation about nature. Many people here can testify to this, and I appeal to them. Those of you who have heard me, tell your neighbors whether you have ever heard me say anything, at length or briefly, about such matters ... You hear their answer. From what they say about this part of the charge, you can judge the truth of the rest.

There is just as little foundation to the report that I teach for money. It is no truer than the other accusation. If someone really could educate people, I would consider it honorable for him to accept payment for teaching. Take Gorgias of Leontium, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. They travel from city to city and persuade young men to leave their own citizens, who could teach them for nothing, and study with them instead. The young men pay them and are even grateful for permission to do so. I have heard of a philosopher from Paros who is staying in Athens at present. Here is how I heard of him. I met Callias, the son of Hipponicus, who has spent a fortune on Sophists. Knowing he had sons, I asked him: 'Callias, if your two sons were colts or calves, we would have no difficulty finding someone to take charge of them. We would hire a horse trainer or a farmer, I suppose, to develop their abilities and make them as good as animals of their kind can be. But they are human beings. Whom do you intend to put in charge of them? Is there anyone who understands what makes a good human being and citizen?

You must have considered this, since you have sons. Is there someone?' 'There is,' he said. 'Who is he?' I asked. 'Where is he from, and what does he charge?' 'Evenus of Paros,' he answered. 'He charges five minae.' Lucky Evenus, I thought, if he really possesses this wisdom and teaches it for so modest a fee. If I had the same knowledge, I would be very proud and full of myself. But the truth is that I have no knowledge of this kind.

Perhaps one of you will say: 'Yes, Socrates, but where do these accusations come from? You must have been doing something unusual. All these rumors and all this talk would never have arisen if you were like other people. Tell us the reason, because we would not want to judge you hastily.' I think that is a fair challenge. I will try to explain why I am called wise and have such a bad reputation. Please listen carefully. Some of you may think I am joking, but I promise to tell you the whole truth. Athenians, my reputation comes from a certain kind of wisdom I possess. What kind? The kind a human being may perhaps attain. To that extent, I am inclined to believe I am wise. The people I mentioned earlier, however, possess a superhuman wisdom that I may be unable to describe because I do not have it myself. Anyone who says I do is lying and damaging my reputation. Here, Athenians, I must ask you not to interrupt, even if what I say sounds extravagant. The words I am about to report are not my own. I will refer you to a trustworthy witness: the god at Delphi. He will tell you whether I have any wisdom and, if so, what kind.

You must have known Chaerephon. He was my friend from an early age and your friend too: he shared the people's recent exile and returned with you. As you know, he was impetuous in everything he did. He went to Delphi and boldly asked the oracle whether — as I said, please do not interrupt — whether anyone was wiser than I was. The Pythian priestess answered that no one was wiser. Chaerephon himself is dead, but his brother is here in court and will confirm that what I say is true.

Why do I mention this? Because I want to explain how I acquired my bad reputation. When I heard the answer, I asked myself: What can the god mean? How am I to interpret his riddle? I know I have no wisdom, great or small. What can he mean by saying I am the wisest of men? Yet he is a god and cannot lie; that would be against his nature. After thinking about it for a long time, I found a way to investigate. If I could find someone wiser than myself, I could go to the god with a refutation and say: 'Here is a man wiser than I am, but you said I was the wisest.' So I went to someone reputed to be wise and examined him. I need not mention his name. He was a politician I had chosen to question, and this was the result. As I spoke to him, I could not help thinking he was not really wise, although many people thought he was and he thought so even more strongly himself. I tried to explain that he thought himself wise without actually being so. That made him hate me, and several of those listening became my enemies too. As I left, I said to myself: Neither of us, I suppose, knows anything truly beautiful and good, but I am better off than he is. He does not know, but thinks he does. I neither know nor think I know.

In that particular respect, then, I seem to have a slight advantage. Next I went to another man with even greater claims to wisdom and reached exactly the same conclusion. I made an enemy of him too, and of many others besides.

Then I went from one person to another, well aware of the hostility I was arousing. I regretted it and feared it, but I felt compelled to continue: the god's word must come first, I thought. I must visit everyone who seemed to know something and discover what the oracle meant. And I swear by the dog, Athenians — for I must tell you the truth — that this was the result: the men with the greatest reputations were almost the most foolish, while others held in less esteem were actually wiser and better. Let me tell you about my wanderings and my Herculean labors, as I may call them. After all those efforts, I could only conclude that the oracle could not be refuted. After the politicians, I went to the poets: writers of tragedy, dithyrambs, and every other kind. Here, I told myself, your ignorance will be exposed at once; now you will find you know less than they do. I took some of the most elaborate passages in their own works and asked what they meant, expecting to learn something. Will you believe me? I am almost ashamed to admit it, but hardly anyone here could not have spoken better about their poems than the poets themselves. I realized that poets create their poetry not through wisdom but through a kind of natural gift and inspiration. They resemble diviners and soothsayers, who also say many fine things without understanding what they mean.

The poets seemed to me to be in just that situation. I also noticed that their poetry led them to believe they were the wisest of men in other matters where they were not wise. So I left, thinking myself better off than they were for the same reason I was better off than the politicians.

Finally I went to the craftsmen. I was conscious that I knew virtually nothing, and I was sure they knew many valuable things. Here I was right. They did know much that I did not, and in that respect they were certainly wiser than me. But I saw that even the good craftsmen made the same mistake as the poets: because they were skilled at their work, they thought they understood all sorts of lofty matters as well. That failing overshadowed their wisdom. So, on the oracle's behalf, I asked myself whether I would rather remain as I was, possessing neither their knowledge nor their ignorance, or be like them in both respects. I answered myself and the oracle that I was better off as I was.

This investigation has earned me many enemies of the worst and most dangerous kind, and has given rise to many slanders. People call me 'wise' because my listeners assume I possess the wisdom I expose as lacking in others. But the truth is, men of Athens, that only God is truly wise. His oracle was meant to show that human wisdom amounts to little or nothing. He wasn't really talking about Socrates — he was using my name as an illustration, as if to say: 'The wisest among you is the one who, like Socrates, recognizes that his wisdom is worthless.' And so I go about the world, obedient to the god, examining anyone — citizen or stranger — who seems wise. When I find they aren't, I demonstrate this in service to the oracle. This work consumes me entirely. I have no time for public affairs or personal business, and I live in absolute poverty because of my devotion to the god.

There is another thing. Young men from wealthy families, with plenty of free time, come to me of their own accord. They enjoy hearing me question people who claim to know things. They often imitate me and start questioning others themselves. They soon discover plenty of people who think they know something but actually know little or nothing. Those they question become angry with me instead of themselves. 'That damned Socrates,' they say, 'that scoundrel who leads the young astray!' If someone asks what evil I do or teach, they do not know and cannot answer. Rather than appear at a loss, they repeat the ready-made accusations used against all philosophers: teaching about things up in the clouds and beneath the earth, believing in no gods, and making the worse case appear the better one. They will not admit the truth: that their pretended knowledge has been exposed. There are many of them; they are ambitious, energetic, united against me, and persuasive speakers. So they have filled your ears with their loud and persistent slanders.

That's why my three accusers — Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon — have attacked me. Meletus speaks for the poets, Anytus for the craftsmen and politicians, Lycon for the orators. As I said at the start, I can't expect to clear away so much accumulated slander in such a short time. This, men of Athens, is the truth — the whole truth. I've hidden nothing and misrepresented nothing. And yet I know my bluntness is exactly what makes them hate me — which itself proves I'm telling the truth. This is the source of the prejudice against me, as you'll discover in any inquiry, now or in the future.

I have said enough in my defense against the first group of accusers. Now I turn to the second, led by Meletus, that good man and true patriot, as he calls himself. I must try to defend myself against them too. Let their formal accusation be read. It runs something like this: Socrates does wrong by corrupting the young and by believing not in the gods of the state but in other, new divinities of his own. That is the charge. Now let us examine its separate points. He says I do wrong and corrupt the young. But I say, Athenians, that Meletus does wrong. He pretends to be serious when he is treating the matter as a joke, eagerly bringing people to trial while feigning zeal and concern for matters in which he has never taken the slightest interest. I will try to prove this to you.
Come here, Meletus, and let me ask you a question. You care deeply about improving the young, don't you?
Yes, I do.

Then tell the judges who improves them. You must know, since you have taken the trouble to discover who corrupts them and have summoned and accused me before this court. Speak up and tell the judges who improves the young. Notice, Meletus, that you are silent and have nothing to say. Isn't that disgraceful, and strong evidence for what I said: that you have no interest in this matter? Speak up, my friend, and tell us who improves them.
The laws.
But that is not what I mean, my good man. I want to know who the person is who, to begin with, knows the laws.
The judges, Socrates — the ones here in court.
What, Meletus? Are you saying the judges can teach the young and make them better?
Absolutely.
All of them, or only some?
All of them.
By the goddess Hera, that is good news! There are plenty of people to improve them, then. And what do you say about the audience? Do they improve the young too?
Yes, they do.
And the members of the council?
Yes, the council members improve them.
What about the members of the assembly — do they corrupt the young? Or do they also improve them?
They improve them.
So every single Athenian improves and elevates the young — everyone except me? I alone corrupt them? Is that really what you're saying?
That is exactly what I'm saying.

Then I am very unfortunate, if you are right. But let me ask you something. What about horses? Does one man harm them while everyone else does them good? Isn't the truth the exact opposite? One man, or at least only a few, can do them good: the horse trainer, that is. Others who handle them tend to harm them instead. Isn't that true of horses and all other animals, Meletus? It certainly is, whether you and Anytus say yes or no. How fortunate the young would be if only one person corrupted them while everyone else improved them! But you, Meletus, have shown clearly enough that you have never given the young any thought. Your indifference is evident in your lack of concern for the very matters you accuse me of.

Now, Meletus, let me ask you another question — by Zeus, I will. Is it better to live among good citizens or bad ones? Answer me, friend — it's not a difficult question. Don't good people benefit their neighbors, and bad people harm them?
Certainly.
Is there anyone who would rather be harmed than helped by the people he lives among? Answer, my good friend: the law requires you to answer. Does anyone want to be harmed?
Certainly not.
When you accuse me of corrupting the young and making them worse, do you claim that I do this intentionally or unintentionally?
Intentionally.

But you have just admitted that good people benefit those around them and bad people harm them. Has your superior wisdom taught you this so early in life, while I, at my age, remain too ignorant to understand that someone I must live among is likely to harm me if I corrupt him? Yet you say I corrupt him, and do so intentionally. You are unlikely ever to convince me or anyone else of that. Either I do not corrupt them, or I do it unintentionally. In either case, you are lying. If my offense is unintentional, the law does not deal with unintentional offenses. You should have spoken to me privately, warned me, and corrected me. Once I knew better, I would surely have stopped doing what I had done without intending it. But you would not speak to me and refused to teach me. Now you bring me before this court, a place for punishment, not instruction.

As I said, Athenians, it must now be quite clear to you that Meletus has not the slightest concern for this matter. Still, I would like to know, Meletus, how I am supposed to corrupt the young. From your indictment, I take you to mean that I teach them not to acknowledge the gods the state acknowledges, but other, new divinities or spiritual beings instead. Those, you say, are the teachings by which I corrupt the young?
Yes, that's exactly what I mean.

Then, by the very gods we are discussing, Meletus, explain more clearly to me and the court what you mean! I still do not understand whether you say I teach other people to acknowledge some gods, and therefore believe in gods myself and am not a complete atheist. In that case, you are not accusing me of atheism, only of believing in gods different from those the city acknowledges. Or do you mean simply that I am an atheist and teach atheism?
The latter. You are a complete atheist.
What an extraordinary claim! Why do you think that, Meletus? Do you mean that, unlike other people, I do not believe the sun and moon are divine?
I assure you, judges, he doesn't — he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth.

My friend Meletus, you seem to think you are accusing Anaxagoras! You must have a poor opinion of the judges if you think them so unread that they do not know these ideas fill the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae. Yet you say the young learn them from Socrates, although they are often presented at the theater, where admission costs at most one drachma. (This probably refers to Aristophanes, who caricatured Anaxagoras' ideas, and Euripides, who borrowed them, as well as other dramatists.) The young can pay their money and then laugh at Socrates if he claims these extraordinary views as his own. So do you really think, Meletus, that I believe in no god?
By Zeus, you believe in absolutely none.

No one will believe you, Meletus, and I am fairly sure you do not believe it yourself. Athenians, I cannot help thinking that Meletus is reckless and impudent and has written this indictment out of sheer mischief and youthful bravado. Hasn't he invented a riddle to test me? He must have said to himself: 'I will see whether the wise Socrates discovers my amusing contradiction, or whether I can fool him and everyone else.' He certainly seems to contradict himself in the indictment. It is as if he said that Socrates is guilty of not believing in the gods and yet of believing in them. That is not how someone speaks when he means the matter seriously.

Athenians, I would like you to join me in examining what I take to be his contradiction. And you, Meletus, must answer. I must also remind the audience of my request: do not cause a disturbance if I speak in my usual way:

Has anyone ever believed in human affairs without believing in human beings, Meletus? ... I wish, Athenians, that he would answer instead of constantly trying to stir up interruptions. Has anyone ever believed in horsemanship without believing in horses, or in flute-playing without believing in flute-players? No, my friend. Since you refuse to answer for yourself, I will answer both you and the court: no one ever has. But please answer the next question. Can someone believe in spiritual and divine powers without believing in spirits or demigods?
He cannot.

How fortunate that, with the court's help, I have got that answer out of you! In your indictment you swear that I teach and believe in divine or spiritual powers. Whether they are new or old does not matter here. I believe in spiritual powers, you say, and swear to it in your formal accusation. But if I believe in divine beings, mustn't I also believe in spirits or demigods? Of course I must, so I may take your silence as agreement. What, then, are spirits or demigods? Aren't they either gods or the children of gods?
Certainly they are.

That is exactly the amusing riddle I say you have invented. If the spirits or demigods are gods, you first say I do not believe in gods and then that I do, since I believe in demigods. If, instead, demigods are the children of gods born outside marriage, whether to nymphs or any other mothers they are said to have, who could believe that the gods do not exist when they have children? You might as well say that mules exist but horses and donkeys do not. Such nonsense, Meletus, can only have been meant to test me. You put it in the indictment because you had nothing real to accuse me of. But you will never convince anyone with the slightest understanding that the same people can believe in divine and superhuman things without believing in gods, demigods, and heroes.

I have said enough in answer to Meletus' charge; no elaborate defense is needed. But I know only too well how many enemies I have made. If I am destroyed, that will be the cause: not Meletus or Anytus, but the world's envy and slander. It has killed many good men and will probably kill many more. There is no danger of my being the last.

Someone may ask: 'Aren't you ashamed, Socrates, of living in a way that might bring you to an untimely end?' I would answer fairly: you're wrong to think that. A person who is good for anything shouldn't calculate the chance of living or dying; they should consider only whether in what they're doing they are acting rightly or wrongly — playing the part of a good person or a bad one. By your logic, the heroes who fell at Troy weren't worth much, and above all the son of Thetis, who despised danger altogether compared with disgrace. When he was eager to slay Hector, his goddess mother said to him that if he avenged his companion Patroclus and killed Hector, he would die himself — 'Fate,' she said, in these or similar words, 'waits for you next after Hector.' Receiving this warning, he utterly despised danger and death, fearing instead to live in dishonor and fail to avenge his friend. 'Let me die forthwith,' he replied, 'and be avenged on my enemy, rather than remain here by the beaked ships, a laughing-stock and a burden on the earth.' Did Achilles give any thought to death and danger? Wherever a person's place is — whether chosen or assigned by a commander — that is where they ought to remain in the hour of danger, thinking not of death but only of disgrace. And this, men of Athens, is a true saying.

It would be strange indeed, Athenians, if I deserted my post now through fear of death or anything else. At Potidaea, Amphipolis, and Delium, I stayed where the generals you chose to command me had placed me and faced death like everyone else. Now the god, as I understand and believe, has commanded me to live as a philosopher, examining myself and others. Should I run away? That would be strange. I could rightly be brought before this court for denying the gods' existence if I disobeyed the oracle through fear of death and imagined myself wise when I was not. For fearing death is a pretense of wisdom, not real wisdom: it is pretending to know the unknown. No one knows whether death, which people fear as the greatest evil, may actually be the greatest good. Isn't it shameful ignorance to think you know what you do not know? Only in this respect do I believe I differ from people generally, and may perhaps claim to be wiser: I know little about the world below, but I do not imagine that I know. Yet I do know that injustice and disobedience to someone better than myself, whether god or human, are wrong and dishonorable. I will never fear or avoid something that may be good rather than something I know to be evil.

So if you let me go now, not persuaded by Anytus — who said that since I had been prosecuted I must be put to death, or else I ought never to have been prosecuted at all, and that if I escape now your sons will all be ruined by listening to my words — if instead you said to me: 'Socrates, this time we will not heed Anytus, and you shall be released, but on one condition: you are not to enquire and speculate in this way any more, and if you are caught doing so again you shall die' — if this were the condition on which you released me, I would reply: Men of Athens, I honor and love you, but I shall obey God rather than you. As long as I have life and strength, I will never cease from practicing and teaching philosophy, exhorting anyone I meet and saying to them in my usual way: 'My friend — a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens — are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard at all?' And if the person I'm arguing with says 'Yes, but I do care,' I don't let them go at once; I proceed to interrogate and examine and cross-examine them, and if I think they have no virtue in them but only claim to, I reproach them for undervaluing the greater and overvaluing the less.

I will say the same to everyone I meet — young and old, citizen and foreigner — but especially to my fellow Athenians, because they are my own people. This is God's command, and I believe no greater good has come to this city than my service to God. All I do is go around urging you — every one of you — not to worry about your bodies or your wealth, but first and foremost about the improvement of your soul. Virtue doesn't come from money; rather, from virtue comes money and every other good thing, both for individuals and for the state. If this teaching corrupts the young, then I am doing harm. But if anyone says my teaching is different from this, they're lying. So, men of Athens, whether you follow Anytus's advice or not — whether you acquit me or convict me — know that I will never change my ways, not even if I have to die many times over.

Athenians, do not interrupt; listen to me. We agreed that you would hear me to the end. I have more to say that may make you want to shout in protest, but I believe hearing it will benefit you, so please do not. I want you to know that if you kill someone like me, you will harm yourselves more than me. Neither Meletus nor Anytus can harm me: a bad person is not permitted to harm someone better than himself. I do not deny that Anytus may have him killed, sent into exile, or deprived of his civil rights. He and others may think he is inflicting great harm. But I disagree. The wrong he himself commits by unjustly taking another person's life is far greater.

I'm not arguing for my own sake now, men of Athens, but for yours — so that you don't sin against God by condemning his gift to you. If you kill me, you won't easily find a replacement. I am — if I may use a ridiculous comparison — like a gadfly attached to the state by God. The state is like a great, noble horse that is sluggish because of its size and needs to be stirred into action. I am that gadfly — constantly landing on you, waking you up, persuading you, challenging you, all day long, everywhere. You won't easily find another like me. I'd advise you to spare me. You might be annoyed — like someone suddenly woken from sleep — and swat me dead, as Anytus suggests. Then you'd sleep peacefully for the rest of your lives, unless God, in his care for you, sent another gadfly. That I was sent by God, you can see from this: no ordinary person would neglect all their own affairs for all these years, patiently watching them go neglected, just to come to each of you individually like a father or older brother, urging you to care about virtue. Such conduct, I say, is contrary to human nature.

If I had gained anything from this, or if my exhortations had been paid for, there would be some explanation. But, as you can see, even my shameless accusers do not dare say that I have ever demanded or sought payment from anyone. They have no witness to that. I, however, have a sufficient witness to the truth of what I say: my poverty.

Someone may wonder why I go around giving advice privately and concerning myself with other people's affairs but do not venture to speak publicly and advise the state. I will tell you why. At various times and places, you have heard me speak of a divine message or sign that comes to me. This is the divinity Meletus ridicules in his indictment. The sign, a kind of voice, first came to me when I was a child. It always stops me from doing something I am about to do, but never urges me to act. This is what keeps me out of politics, and rightly, I think. I am certain, Athenians, that if I had entered politics I would have died long ago without benefiting you or myself. Do not be offended when I tell you the truth: no one who opposes you or any other crowd, honestly resisting the many lawless and unjust deeds committed in a state, will save his life. Anyone who fights for what is right must do so as a private citizen rather than a public official if he wants to survive even for a short time.

I can give convincing evidence for what I say, not just words but what you value much more: actions. Let me tell you about an episode in my own life. It will show that I would never yield to injustice through fear of death, and that by refusing to yield I would have faced immediate death. It is a story about legal proceedings, perhaps not very interesting, but true. The only public office I ever held, Athenians, was as a council member. My tribe, Antiochis, held the presidency during the trial of the generals who had failed to recover the dead after the battle of Arginusae. You proposed trying them together, contrary to law, as you all recognized afterward. At the time, I alone among the Prytanes, the council's presiding members, opposed the illegality and voted against you. The speakers threatened to impeach and arrest me, and you shouted. But I decided to risk it with law and justice on my side rather than join in your injustice through fear of imprisonment or death. That happened under the democracy. Later, when the oligarchy of the Thirty held power, they summoned me and four others to the rotunda and ordered us to bring Leon of Salamis from Salamis, because they wanted to execute him.

This was typical of the commands the Thirty issued — they wanted to involve as many people as possible in their crimes. But I showed, not just in words but in action, that I didn't care a straw for death, if I may put it that way — my only concern was never to do anything unjust or unholy. The threat of that oppressive regime didn't frighten me into wrongdoing. When we left the rotunda, the other four went to Salamis and arrested Leon. I went quietly home. I might have been killed for that, if the Thirty hadn't fallen from power shortly after. Many witnesses can confirm this.

Do you really imagine I could have survived all these years in public life if, like a good man, I had always upheld what was right and put justice first, as I should? Certainly not, Athenians: neither I nor anyone else. But I have always been consistent in my actions, public and private. I have never dishonorably given in to those slanderously called my pupils or to anyone else. In fact, I have no regular pupils. But anyone, young or old, who wants to listen while I pursue my mission is welcome. Nor do I speak only with those who pay. Anyone, rich or poor, may question me, answer me, and hear what I say. Whether he turns out good or bad cannot fairly be attributed to me, since I never taught or claimed to teach him anything. If anyone says he has privately learned or heard something from me that everyone else has not heard, he is lying.

But someone will ask: Why do people enjoy continually talking with you? I have already told you the whole truth about that, Athenians. They enjoy hearing me question people who claim to be wise; it is entertaining. The god has imposed this duty on me and made it known through oracles, visions, and every way in which a divine power has ever communicated its will. This is true, Athenians; if it were not, it would soon be disproved. If I am corrupting the young or have done so, those who are now grown up and realize I gave them bad advice in their youth should come forward to accuse me and take their revenge. If they do not want to come themselves, their fathers, brothers, or other relatives should tell you what harm I have done their families. Now is their chance. I see many of them here in court. There is Crito, who is my age and comes from the same deme, or local district, and I also see his son Critobulus. Here is Lysanias of Sphettus, the father of Aeschines, and Antiphon of Cephisus, the father of Epigenes. There are also brothers of several men who have spent time with me.

There is Nicostratus, son of Theosdotides and brother of Theodotus. Theodotus himself is dead, so at least he will not try to stop him. There is Paralus, son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages, and Adeimantus, son of Ariston, whose brother Plato is present. There is also Aeantodorus, brother of Apollodorus, whom I see as well. I could name many more. Meletus should have called some of them as witnesses during his speech. If he forgot, let him call them now; I will give way to him. Let him say whether he has any testimony of that kind to offer. No, Athenians, the truth is the exact opposite. All these people are ready to testify for the man Meletus and Anytus call the corrupter and injurer of their relatives. Not just the supposedly corrupted young men, who might have a motive for doing so, but their uncorrupted older relatives too. Why should they support me with their testimony? Why, except for truth and justice, and because they know I am telling the truth and Meletus is lying?

Well, Athenians, these and similar considerations are all the defense I have to offer. But one more word. Someone may resent me when he remembers how, in a similar or even less serious case, he prayed and pleaded with the judges in tears. Perhaps he brought his children into court to stir their pity, along with a crowd of relatives and friends. Yet I, whose life is probably at stake, will do none of that. The contrast may turn him against me and make him vote in anger. If anyone here feels this way, and I am not saying anyone does, I can fairly reply: My friend, I too am a human being of flesh and blood, not 'of wood or stone,' as Homer says. I have a family and sons, Athenians, three of them: one nearly grown and two still young. Yet I will bring none of them here to beg you for an acquittal. Why not? Not out of pride or disrespect for you. Whether I fear death is another question, which I will not discuss now. But, considering our public reputation, I think such conduct would disgrace me, you, and the whole state. A man of my age and reputation for wisdom should not demean himself in that way.

Whether that reputation is deserved or not, people have decided that Socrates is somehow superior to other men. How shameful, then, if those among you thought outstanding in wisdom, courage, or any other virtue demean themselves in this way! I have seen respected men behave very strangely when convicted. They seemed to imagine that death would be something terrible and that they could be immortal if only you let them live. I think they dishonor the state. Any foreigner who came in would say that Athens' leading men, whom the Athenians themselves honor and place in command, are no better than women. Those of us with reputations should not behave like that, and if we do, you should not allow it. You should show that you are much more willing to convict someone who stages a pitiful scene and makes the city ridiculous than someone who remains quiet.

But even setting public opinion aside, it seems wrong to ask a judge for a favor and obtain an acquittal that way, instead of informing and convincing him. His duty is to give judgment, not to hand out justice as a gift. He has sworn to judge according to the laws, not his own wishes. We should not encourage you to break that oath, and you should not let yourselves be encouraged to do so. There can be no piety in that. So do not ask me to do what I consider dishonorable, impious, and wrong, especially now that Meletus is prosecuting me for impiety. If persuasion and pleading enabled me to overcome your oaths, Athenians, I would be teaching you to believe that the gods do not exist. My defense would then convict me of the very charge of not believing in them. But that is not the case; quite the contrary. I believe the gods exist in a higher sense than any of my accusers. I leave my case to you and to the god, for you to decide as is best for you and me.

chapters.title: The Penalty
paragraphs: I have many reasons not to be upset, men of Athens, at your vote of condemnation. I expected it. What surprises me is how close the vote was — I thought the majority against me would be much larger. If just thirty votes had gone the other way, I would have been acquitted. And against Meletus specifically, I think I've clearly won. Without the help of Anytus and Lycon, he wouldn't have received a fifth of the votes, and the law would have required him to pay a fine of a thousand drachmas.

So he proposes the death penalty. What should I propose instead? What do I actually deserve? What should be given to a man who has never been idle, who has ignored the things most people chase — wealth, business, military rank, political office, all the clubs and factions — because he was too honest to survive in politics? Instead, I went where I could do the most good: to each of you individually, trying to persuade every person to care about becoming wise and virtuous before caring about personal interests, and to improve the state before seeking benefits from it. What does such a person deserve? Something good, I think — something fitting. What reward suits a poor man who has been your benefactor and who needs the time to keep instructing you? Nothing would be more fitting than free meals at the Prytaneum — a reward he deserves far more than an Olympic chariot winner. That person gives you the appearance of happiness; I give you the real thing.

I'm poor, and the Olympic winner has plenty. He gives you the appearance of happiness; I give you the reality. If I'm to suggest a fair penalty, I'd say free meals at the Prytaneum is the right answer.

You might think I'm being defiant, just as I was when I spoke about tears and entreaties. I'm not. It's that I'm convinced I never deliberately wronged anyone — though I can't convince you, because we've had too little time together. If Athenian law allowed capital cases to be decided over several days, as it does in other cities, I believe I could have persuaded you. But I can't refute years of slander in a moment. Since I know I've never wronged another person, I certainly won't wrong myself by admitting I deserve punishment. Why should I? To avoid the death penalty Meletus proposes? I don't even know if death is good or bad — why would I propose a punishment I know to be bad? Prison? Why should I live as a slave to whatever magistrate happens to hold office? A fine, with prison until it's paid? Same problem — I have no money. Exile? I'd have to be blind with love of life to think that strangers would tolerate the conversations that my own fellow citizens couldn't bear.

Someone would say: 'Can't you just stop talking, Socrates, and live quietly in exile?' This is the hardest thing for me to explain to you. If I told you that remaining silent would be disobedience to God, you wouldn't believe me. And if I said that examining life is the greatest human good — that the unexamined life is not worth living — you'd believe me even less. Yet what I say is true, even though it's hard to make you see it. I've never thought I deserved to suffer harm. If I had money, I'd propose a fine I could pay without real hardship. But I have nothing. Well — perhaps I could manage one mina, so let that be my penalty. But wait — Plato, Crito, Critobulus, and Apollodorus are telling me to say thirty minas, and they'll guarantee it. So let thirty minas be the fine — they're good for it.

No, let me reconsider. Someone would say: 'Can't you just keep quiet and go somewhere else?' This is the hardest point for you to understand. If I tell you that to do as you say would be disobedience to God, you won't believe me. And if I say that the greatest good for a person is to discuss virtue every day — that the unexamined life is not worth living — you'll believe me even less. Yet this is the truth, hard as it is to accept. I've never believed I deserved harm. If I had money, I'd propose a manageable fine. But I don't. Perhaps I could scrape together one mina. But Plato, Crito, Critobulus, and Apollodorus are urging me to say thirty minas — they'll be my guarantors. Let thirty minas be the penalty; they're reliable sureties.

chapters.title: Final Words
paragraphs: You haven't gained much time, men of Athens, and you've earned a terrible reputation. The city's critics will say you killed Socrates — a wise man (they'll call me wise to spite you, even if I'm not). If you had waited just a little while, nature would have done the job for you. I'm old, as you can see — close to death already. I'm speaking now only to those who voted to condemn me. You may think I lost because I couldn't find the right words. Not at all. What I lacked wasn't words but shamelessness — the willingness to say and do whatever would please you: weeping, wailing, begging, and all the undignified behavior you're used to hearing from others. I thought then, and I think now, that a person in danger shouldn't stoop to anything base. I would rather die having spoken in my own way than live having spoken in yours. In war and in court alike, a person shouldn't use every possible means to escape death.

In battle, anyone can save their life by throwing down their weapons and begging their pursuers for mercy. In every dangerous situation, there are ways to cheat death — if you're willing to say and do anything. The hard thing isn't avoiding death; it's avoiding wrongdoing, because wrongdoing runs faster than death. I am old and slow, and the slower runner — death — has caught me. My accusers are young and fast, and the faster runner — wickedness — has caught them. I leave this court sentenced to death by you; they leave sentenced to depravity and injustice by truth itself. I accept my sentence; let them accept theirs. Perhaps this is how it had to be. I think it's fair.

Now, to those who condemned me, I want to make a prophecy — for in the hour of death, people are gifted with prophetic power. I tell you, my executioners: the moment I'm gone, a punishment far heavier than what you've given me will fall on you. You killed me because you wanted to avoid being questioned, to avoid giving an account of your lives. But it won't work out that way. There will be more people questioning you than before — people I've been holding back. They're younger and will be harsher, and you'll be even more offended. If you think killing people will stop them from criticizing your lives, you're wrong. That escape route is neither possible nor honorable. The easiest and noblest path is not to silence others but to improve yourselves. That is my prophecy to those who condemned me.

To my friends who voted to acquit me, I'd like to talk about what has just happened, while we have time before I go to my death. Stay with me a moment — we can talk while it's still possible. I want to tell you something remarkable. Throughout my life, my divine sign — that inner voice — has constantly opposed me, even in trivial matters, whenever I was about to make a mistake. Yet today, facing what most people consider the ultimate evil, the sign didn't oppose me at all — not when I left home this morning, not when I came to court, not during anything I said. In the past, it has often stopped me mid-sentence. But today it raised no objection to anything I said or did. What do I make of this? I'll tell you: it suggests that what has happened to me is actually good. Those of us who think death is evil must be wrong. My sign would certainly have stopped me if I had been heading toward harm.

Consider it this way, and there's strong reason to hope that death is good. Death is one of two things: either it's a state of complete nothingness and unconsciousness, or it's a journey to another place where the dead reside. If it's dreamless sleep, then death is an extraordinary gain. Think about it: if someone picked the night in which they slept so soundly they didn't even dream, and compared it with all the other nights and days of their life — even a great king would find very few days or nights more pleasant than that one. If death is like that, it's pure gain — eternity becomes a single peaceful night. But if death is a journey to another place where all the dead gather, what could be better? Imagine arriving where the pretend judges of this world have no power, and finding the true judges — Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and every other righteous soul. Wouldn't that journey be worth making?

What would you give to talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer? If this is true, let me die again and again! I'd find it wonderful to meet Palamedes, Ajax, and every hero who suffered an unjust death — comparing my experience with theirs would be endlessly fascinating. Best of all, I could continue doing what I do now: examining people. What would you give to question the leaders of the Trojan War, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, or countless others — men and women both? The joy of conversing with them and examining them would be beyond measure. And in that world, they certainly don't execute people for asking questions. The dead are not only happier than the living but, if what we're told is true, they're immortal.

So be of good cheer about death, my judges, and remember this truth: no evil can befall a good person, in life or in death. The gods do not neglect such a person. What has happened to me hasn't happened by accident. I see clearly that it was better for me to die now and be released from trouble. That's why my divine sign never stopped me today. I bear no anger toward my accusers or those who condemned me. They haven't actually harmed me, even though they didn't intend to help me. For that, I may gently criticize them.

But I do have one favor to ask. When my sons are grown, I ask you, my friends, to give them the same trouble I've given you — if they seem to care more about money or anything else than about virtue, or if they pretend to be something they're not. Challenge them as I've challenged you, for not caring about what truly matters and for thinking they're someone when they're nothing. If you do this, both I and my sons will have been treated justly.
The hour of departure has come. We go our separate ways — I to die, and you to live. Which of us goes to the better fate, only God knows.
